title: The Tea We Make
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
The first batch was undrinkable.

I discovered this before Iroh did because I made the mistake of testing the kettle while he was arguing with the garden door.

Not with a person behind it. With the door.

“Not one more inch,” he told the swollen wooden frame. “You are a door, not a wall. Behave accordingly.”

I took another cautious sip.

The tea tasted as though somebody had boiled a citrus tree and asked it to apologize.

“Iroh?”

“Yes?”

“How do you feel about vinegar?”

He appeared in the kitchen immediately.

“Vinegar?”

“Because I think we've invented a very expensive one.”

He tasted the tea.

I had seen him face difficult questions, old enemies, and a nephew whose temper could melt roofing tiles. I had never seen him look quite so betrayed by a cup.

“Oh,” he said.

“That's diplomatic.”

“It is surprising.”

“That's also diplomatic.”

He set the cup down with care. “We shall not offer this to guests.”

“Or enemies.”

Iroh gave me an appraising look. “You continue to underestimate how cruel you can be.”

The Jasmine Dragon was quiet that morning. The chairs had been turned upside down on the tables, and a streak of pale sunlight stretched across the floor from the high window. In the courtyard, the vines we'd planted along the rear wall had begun to climb the trellis. A month earlier, Iroh had called them weeds. Now he watered them himself and denied having any favorites.

We were making a new tea blend.

That sounded like a small thing. It had taken us three weeks of conversations, two ruined baskets of leaves, and one spectacular argument about whether smoke-dried peel belonged in a civilized teapot.

It was supposed to be something we could both claim.

I had insisted that mattered.

Iroh knew a hundred years of history in the shape of a leaf. He could tell which hillside grew it, when to pick it, how hot the water should be. He had learned to respect traditions that survived empires.

I knew less. I knew how to taste what was there and admit when I wanted something different. The Vale had given us a fragrant vine whose leaves resembled neither tea nor any herb I recognized. Iroh wouldn't call it tea.

“Then we'll call it part of a blend,” I had said.

“A botanical misunderstanding.”

“A delicious botanical misunderstanding.”

That remained to be proved.

At midmorning a young delivery worker named Tali arrived with a basket of dried jasmine and a question about the new jar labels. She was curious about our experiment because her mother worked at a small medical dispensary and had heard someone describe the vine as good for fever.

“Is it?” she asked.

“No,” I said.

Iroh turned from the counter. “We have no evidence that it is.”

Tali frowned. “But people are saying it.”

“Then we must give them a more accurate story,” he said.

It was such an ordinary answer. But it mattered. The shop had survived the war partly because people trusted the man behind its counter. He would not let affection for the Vale become permission to invent cures.

We wrote a label together: jasmine, mild roasted leaf, smoke-dried peel, and the new vine, which we named by its garden name rather than pretending to know an ancient pedigree.

Tali watched us argue over the order of ingredients.

“You two do this often?”

“Yes,” I said.

“No,” Iroh said at the same time.

She laughed.

“Usually,” he corrected, “we arrive at a very wise decision.”

“After arguing.”

“After discussing.”

“After arguing with tea.”

He folded his arms. “The tea rarely listens.”

When Tali left, I noticed Iroh studying the fresh labels. His thumb rested against the paper while his other hand remained near the old wooden tea box he kept behind the register.

“What is it?” I asked.

He shook his head.

I knew better than to turn that into permission to guess. I continued measuring the roasted leaves while he considered whether to speak.

At length he said, “Lu Ten liked to invent ridiculous names for ordinary things.”

I stopped.

“He once called a poorly packed travel chest a mobile disaster,” Iroh continued. “He was not wrong. We lost half our dinner on the road.”

I pictured the two of them, younger, laughing at a spilled meal. It was not a memory I owned. It was a gift I had been offered.

“Did he like tea?” I asked.

“He liked my company. He tolerated the tea.”

That broke something tender open in his voice. He smiled at the box as though the smile could reach backward.

I did not tell him I was sorry. We both knew what I was sorry for. Instead I asked whether he'd like to keep the box where it was.

“Yes,” he said.

I set the label beside it.

After a moment he reached across the counter and brushed the back of my fingers. I turned my hand over. He held it, then let go when he needed both hands for the sieve.

The next batch began with less peel.

We tasted it.

“Better,” I said.

“Much.”

“Needs more of the vine.”

“Everything doesn't require novelty.”

“Everything doesn't require a history lesson.”

His eyebrows rose. It was not anger. It was the surprise of discovering we had stumbled onto the actual argument.

I set down the spoon.

“You're allowed to prefer the older blend,” I said. “But I don't want to make something ‘ours’ if the only pieces of me in it are the parts you already know how to use.”

Iroh was quiet.

The kitchen window rattled in a gust of wind. A cart rolled past outside. The ordinary world refused to wait for either of us to produce a perfect answer.

At last he said, “I have asked you to learn so many of my customs. Perhaps I have not asked often enough which ones you wish to bring.”

I glanced at the small jar of smoke-dried peel.

“I don't want the past thrown out,” I said. “I like that you know how to keep it. I just want room for us to make mistakes without calling them disrespect.”

He looked at our failed first batch.

“Then we are doing very well,” he said.

I laughed despite myself.

We made a third pot. I adjusted the vine. Iroh changed the water temperature. We agreed to record both changes so neither of us could claim an imaginary victory later.

The result smelled like jasmine opening in warm rain, with a sharp bright edge that lingered behind the sweetness.

I took one sip, then another.

Iroh watched me over his cup.

“Well?” he asked.

“We might have made something.”

“Something?”

“Do you want to give it a grand name, or shall we admit we're still testing it?”

He considered. “I was thinking ‘Second Beginning.’”

That made my chest tighten.

“Too sentimental?” he asked.

“Maybe a little.”

“Then you name it.”

I looked at the paper scattered across the counter: three failed measurements, two different hands, a note telling us not to claim medicinal properties, and a tiny ink stain from the moment I had knocked over the bottle.

“The Tea We Make,” I said.

He smiled.

“Perhaps,” he said, “that is the wiser name.”

We placed the jar beside the register. He wrote the first half of the label. I wrote the second. Our handwriting looked nothing alike; it was not supposed to.

When the shop opened, Tali returned and tried a small cup. She made a face at the new flavor, then asked for another.

“An excellent review,” Iroh announced.

“She hasn't said a word.”

“Some things do not require words.”

“Careful. You say that too often, and I'll stop asking what you mean.”

He leaned toward me. “I would miss your questions.”

The last customers left at dusk. I found him in the kitchen, sitting at last, the new jar within reach. He had been saving a final cup for the two of us.

I kissed him over the table.

He startled, then laughed softly into my mouth. When I drew back, he brushed a strand of hair away from my cheek and waited.

“Another cup?” he asked.

“Later.”

“Ah,” he said. “A dangerous answer.”

I took his hand. We left the jar on the counter and went upstairs together, allowing the rest of the evening to belong to us alone.

In the morning the handwriting was still there. Two hands, two histories, one recipe neither of us would have reached without the other.

I made the first pot.

Iroh tasted it, considered, and reached for the peel.

“Don't,” I warned.

His smile was enormous.

“I was only going to look.”

“Liar.”

“A teacher, perhaps.”

“Not today.”

He set down the peel.

For once, he let me lead.
